title: Pitot-Static and Vacuum Systems — How Instruments Work and How They Fail

required_knowledge_points.title: Pitot-Static System — Which Instruments Use What Pressure
required_knowledge_points.why: The DPE asks: 'Your pitot tube is clogged by ice. Which instruments are affected?' The student who says 'the whole panel' has failed. The correct granular answer: only the airspeed indicator uses BOTH pitot and static. Altimeter and VSI use STATIC ONLY. The DPE then follows: 'With a clogged pitot and open static, what does the airspeed indicator do in a climb?' This is a multi-step inference most students fail.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: Pitot-static instrument system: PITOT TUBE: measures total (ram) air pressure — the impact pressure of the air as the aircraft moves forward. STATIC PORT: measures ambient (undisturbed atmospheric) pressure. Typically located flush on the fuselage side. Which instruments use which source: (1) AIRSPEED INDICATOR (ASI): uses BOTH pitot pressure (impact) AND static pressure (reference). ASI measures the DIFFERENCE: ram pressure minus static = dynamic pressure = airspeed. (2) ALTIMETER: uses STATIC ONLY. Measures absolute static pressure and converts to altitude using the ISA model. No pitot input. (3) VERTICAL SPEED INDICATOR (VSI): uses STATIC ONLY. Measures the RATE of change in static pressure (the case reference bleeds through a calibrated leak). No pitot input. Blocked pitot scenarios: (1) PITOT BLOCKED, STATIC OPEN: ASI shows erroneous reading (no ram input). If pitot drain hole is clear, ASI reads zero. If drain hole also blocked, ASI freezes at the altitude where blockage occurred, then OVER-READS in a climb (pressure trapped in pitot line remains constant; static drops with altitude; the differential increases = false higher airspeed). (2) STATIC BLOCKED, PITOT OPEN: ASI, altimeter, and VSI all stop at the values at the altitude of blockage. Altimeter freezes. VSI reads zero. ASI under-reads in a climb (pitot increases with speed; static line pressure is stuck at blocked-altitude pressure = lower differential = lower apparent airspeed).
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### Pressure Sources
| Source | Measures | Location |
|---|---|---|
| **Pitot Tube** | Total (ram) air pressure — impact of forward motion | Nose or wing leading edge |
| **Static Port** | Ambient (undisturbed atmospheric) pressure | Flush-mounted on fuselage |

### Which Instruments Use Which Source
| Instrument | Pitot | Static | What It Measures |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Airspeed Indicator (ASI)** | ✅ Yes | ✅ Yes | Difference (dynamic pressure) = airspeed |
| **Altimeter** | ❌ No | ✅ Yes | Absolute static pressure = altitude |
| **VSI** | ❌ No | ✅ Yes | Rate of static pressure change = climb/descent rate |

### Blockage Failure Modes

#### Pitot Blocked, Static Open
| Condition | ASI Behavior | Altimeter/VSI |
|---|---|---|
| Drain hole **open** | Reads **zero** (no ram input) | Normal ✅ |
| Drain hole **also blocked** | **Freezes, then OVER-READS** in climb (trapped pressure vs. dropping static = rising differential) | Normal ✅ |

#### Static Blocked, Pitot Open
| Instrument | Behavior |
|---|---|
| **ASI** | **Under-reads** in climb (pitot increases; static frozen = lower differential) |
| **Altimeter** | **Freezes** at altitude of blockage |
| **VSI** | **Reads zero** (no pressure change reference) |

> ⚠️ **Checkride Trap:** Blocked pitot with sealed drain = ASI **rises in a climb even though airspeed may be constant**. This has caused fatal crashes. Pitot heat prevents this — activate it **before** entering visible moisture.

required_knowledge_points.title: Pitot Heat and Alternate Static Source — Blockage Prevention and Recovery
required_knowledge_points.why: The DPE asks: 'When do you use pitot heat? When do you use alternate static?' These are operational decisions, not just factual recalls. Pitot heat is required in IMC or icing conditions — understand when to turn it on and that it is PREVENTIVE (not always a fix when ice has already accumulated). Alternate static is the response to a blocked static port — know the instrument behavior change that accompanies the switch.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: Pitot heat: electrically heated element inside the pitot tube prevents ice accumulation. Must be active BEFORE entering visible moisture or icing conditions — ice can block the pitot tube in seconds. Turning pitot heat on AFTER icing may not clear accumulated ice rapidly. Required to be checked ON before IMC flight in most operations. Method verification: pitot heat ON → ammeter shows a small increase in electrical draw (3-5 amps) confirming the heating element is working. Ice accretion on pitot: indicates icing conditions present; turn on carburetor heat simultaneously if applicable to prevent carb ice. Alternate static source: a back-up port inside the cockpit (most aircraft) or on an alternate fuselage location. Activated by a pull knob or valve in the cockpit. When used: static port is blocked or suspected blocked. Effect: cabin pressure vs. normal static pressure differential. Cabin pressure is slightly LOWER than outside static pressure (due to cabin pressurization from ram effects and aircraft design). When alternate static is selected in an unpressurized aircraft: (1) Altimeter reads HIGHER than actual altitude (cabin slightly lower pressure than outside static). (2) ASI reads SLIGHTLY HIGHER than actual airspeed. (3) VSI briefly shows a climb then returns to current vertical speed. Pilot must account for this altitude over-read when shooting approaches in IMC with alternate static active.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### Pitot Heat
- **Electrically heated element** inside the pitot tube — prevents ice accumulation
- Must be activated **BEFORE** entering visible moisture or icing conditions
- Turning it on **after** ice has formed may not clear blockage rapidly

**Verification:** Pitot heat ON → **ammeter draw increases 3–5 amps** confirming the heating element is functioning

> ⚠️ **Checkride Trap:** Pitot heat is **preventive** — not a guaranteed de-icing tool. Icing conditions also mean activating **carburetor heat** (if carbureted engine) simultaneously.

### Alternate Static Source
- **Backup static port** — located inside cockpit (most aircraft) or alternate fuselage location
- **When to use:** Static port is blocked or suspected blocked
- **Activated by:** Pull knob or valve in cockpit

### Instrument Behavior After Switching to Alternate Static
| Instrument | Effect | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **Altimeter** | Reads **HIGHER** than actual altitude | Cabin pressure is slightly **lower** than outside ambient static |
| **ASI** | Reads **slightly higher** than actual airspeed | Same lower-pressure reference effect |
| **VSI** | Brief **climb indication**, then returns to actual rate | Pressure equalization from switch |

> ⚠️ **Checkride Trap:** When shooting an approach in IMC with alternate static active, the altimeter **over-reads** — account for this during final approach. The DPE will ask: *'What effect does alternate static have on the altimeter?'* Answer: reads **higher** than actual.

required_knowledge_points.title: Vacuum System — Which Instruments It Powers and Gyro Failure Modes
required_knowledge_points.why: The DPE asks: 'Your vacuum system fails. Which instruments are affected?' The correct answer must be specific: Attitude Indicator (AI) and Heading Indicator (HI) are vacuum-gyro instruments in most light aircraft. The Turn Coordinator (TC) is electrically powered. So in a vacuum failure, the AI and HI fail — but the TC survives. This is the partial panel scenario — and the DPE often follows up by asking about the TC's function in partial panel.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: Vacuum system: engine-driven vacuum pump creates suction (approximately 4.5-5.5 in. Hg). This suction spins the gyroscope rotors inside gyro instruments at high RPM (thousands of revolutions per minute). Vacuum pump failure: suction drops → gyros slow down → instruments precess (drift from true indication) → eventually become erratic and fail. NOT immediate: gyros continue for a time after vacuum failure on residual spin — instruments may appear normal for several minutes before becoming clearly unreliable. Critical vacuum failure diagnostic: check the suction gauge (in. Hg). Normal: 4.5-5.5 in. Hg. Vacuum-powered instruments: (1) ATTITUDE INDICATOR (AI): vacuum gyro — fails with vacuum loss. Shows pitch and bank attitude. Tumbles or precesses to erroneous attitude after vacuum failure. (2) HEADING INDICATOR (HI/DI): vacuum gyro — fails with vacuum loss. Shows aircraft heading via gyroscopic rigidity. Drifts after vacuum failure. Electrically-powered instruments that SURVIVE vacuum failure: (1) TURN COORDINATOR (TC): electrically powered gyro. Shows RATE of turn and bank direction. Survives vacuum failure intact. (2) Magnetic compass: no power required — survives all electrical and vacuum failures. Available as the ultimate heading reference. Partial panel operations (vacuum failure): fly using TC + altimeter + ASI + magnetic compass. The TC replaces the AI for maintaining wings-level and detecting turns.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### Vacuum System
- Engine-driven **vacuum pump** creates suction (~**4.5–5.5 in. Hg**)
- Suction spins **gyroscope rotors** inside gyro instruments at thousands of RPM

### Vacuum-Powered vs. Electrically-Powered Instruments
| Instrument | Power Source | Fails with Vacuum Loss? |
|---|---|---|
| **Attitude Indicator (AI)** | Vacuum gyro | ✅ **YES** — tumbles or precesses |
| **Heading Indicator (HI/DI)** | Vacuum gyro | ✅ **YES** — drifts then fails |
| **Turn Coordinator (TC)** | Electrical | ❌ **NO** — survives vacuum failure |
| **Magnetic Compass** | No power required | ❌ **NO** — always available |

### Vacuum Failure — The Slow-Motion Trap
- Gyros do **NOT** stop immediately — they spin down on **residual energy**
- AI and HI may appear **normal for several minutes** before precessing to obviously false readings
- **Diagnostic:** Monitor the **suction gauge** — normal = 4.5–5.5 in. Hg

> ⚠️ **Checkride Trap:** An AI that looks normal may already be **drifting** after vacuum loss. A pilot not monitoring the suction gauge can follow a false attitude into IMC. Check the suction gauge regularly.

### Partial Panel Operations (After Vacuum Failure)
Navigate using:
1. **Turn Coordinator** — bank and rate information (replaces AI)
2. **Altimeter** — altitude reference
3. **ASI** — energy state
4. **Magnetic compass** — heading (with known acceleration/turning errors)

required_knowledge_points.title: Magnetic Compass Errors — Acceleration and Turning Errors in the Northern Hemisphere
required_knowledge_points.why: The DPE asks: 'If you make a rapid acceleration during takeoff roll, what does the magnetic compass indicate?' Most students guess 'it stays accurate — it's a direct magnetic reference.' Wrong: the pendulous vane and liquid compass have acceleration and turning errors that produce false readings. Knowing ANDS for acceleration and OSSC for turning errors is required checkride knowledge.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: Magnetic compass errors: (1) MAGNETIC DIP: compass needle is attracted toward the earth's magnetic field lines, which dip downward at higher latitudes. Creates errors during turns and accelerations. (2) ACCELERATION ERROR (ANDS — Accelerate North, Decelerate South, in northern hemisphere): During acceleration on an easterly or westerly heading: the compass erroneously shows a NORTH turn. During deceleration on an east/west heading: the compass erroneously shows a SOUTH turn. Mnemonic: ANDS (Accelerate North, Decelerate South). Most pronounced on east/west headings, negligible on north/south. (3) TURNING ERROR (OSSC — Overshoot South, Undershoot North, in northern hemisphere): During turns THROUGH NORTH: compass lags behind the actual heading change — the pilot must UNDERSHOOT (stop before north) then the compass catches up. Wait — corrected: when rolling out TO North, stop EARLY (before the compass reads north) because the compass will continue turning north. When rolling out TO South, stop LATE (after the compass reads south) because the compass lags. Mnemonic correctly stated: Undershoot North, Overshoot South. HSI (Horizontal Situation Indicator): gyroscopic heading indicator — does NOT have these errors. But must be aligned to the magnetic compass periodically (drifts, requires re-syncing every 15-20 minutes in cruise).
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### Why the Magnetic Compass Has Errors
- The compass needle is attracted to the Earth's magnetic field, which **dips downward** at higher latitudes (**magnetic dip**)
- This dip causes systematic errors during **acceleration** and **turns**

### Acceleration Error — Mnemonic: **ANDS**
*(Northern Hemisphere, on East/West headings)*

| Action | Compass Shows |
|---|---|
| **Accelerate** on E/W heading | False turn toward **N**orth |
| **Decelerate** on E/W heading | False turn toward **S**outh |

> **ANDS = Accelerate North, Decelerate South**
> - Negligible on North/South headings — most pronounced on East/West

### Turning Error — Mnemonic: **UN-OS**
*(Northern Hemisphere)*

| Rolling out TO... | Compass Behavior | Pilot Action |
|---|---|---|
| **North** | Compass **lags** (reads less than actual heading) | Roll out **early** (Undershoot North) |
| **South** | Compass **leads** (reads more than actual heading) | Roll out **late** (Overshoot South) |

> ⚠️ **Checkride Trap:** When turning to north, the compass can falsely indicate you've already passed north — so you stop the turn too early. Answer: roll out **before** the compass reaches north.

### HSI (Horizontal Situation Indicator)
- **Gyroscopic** — no acceleration or turning errors
- Must be **re-synced to magnetic compass** every **15–20 minutes** in cruise (gyro drift)

lesson_overview:
## Pitot-Static and Vacuum Systems -- When the Instruments Lie and Why

Instrument systems fail in specific and predictable ways. The pilot who understands the mechanism can diagnose which system is compromised, interpret the remaining instruments correctly, and make the right decisions. The pilot who only knows procedures -- 'turn on pitot heat if icing' -- is helpless when the ice has already formed and the airspeed is doing something unexpected. This lesson is about mechanism -- why each failure mode produces the exact instrument behavior it does.

**The pressure architecture: who uses what.** Three flight instruments derive their readings from the pitot-static system. The ASI uses both pitot pressure and static pressure -- it measures the DIFFERENCE between them, which equals dynamic pressure, which equals airspeed. The altimeter uses only static pressure -- it converts absolute ambient pressure to an altitude reading using the ISA model and the altimeter setting. The VSI uses only static pressure -- specifically, the RATE of pressure change measured through a calibrated leak in the instrument case. This architecture determines the failure signature for every possible blockage scenario.

**Pitot tube blocked, static port open.** The ASI receives no ram air. If the pitot drain hole is open: the ram side equalized to ambient, the differential collapses, ASI reads zero or very low. If the drain hole is ALSO blocked: the air pressure trapped in the pitot line is constant. As the aircraft climbs, outside static pressure drops. The denominator (static) decreases while the numerator (pitot, trapped at the pressure of the altitude where blockage occurred) stays constant -- the differential INCREASES. The ASI shows a rising airspeed in a climb even though actual airspeed may be unchanged. This is the 'frozen pitot with sealed drain' scenario -- and it has caused crashes. The altimeter and VSI are unaffected (static port clear). Pitot heat prevents this: the heating element melts ice before it can block the tube. Turn it ON before entering visible moisture.

**Static port blocked, pitot port open.** All three instruments are affected. The altimeter freezes at the altitude where blockage occurred. The VSI freezes at zero (no pressure change in the reference circuit). The ASI shows a false reading: in a climb, ram pressure increases but static pressure is stuck at the blocked value -- the differential narrows, making it appear airspeed is decreasing even in a climb at constant speed. In a descent, the opposite: ASI over-reads because static is frozen below actual ambient. The alternate static source (a small valve or pull knob that connects the static instruments to cabin air) is the immediate corrective action. Cabin air is slightly lower pressure than outside static -- the altimeter will read slightly HIGH when alternate static is activated. Factor this into your instrument picture.

**Vacuum system failure: the slow-motion trap.** The vacuum pump drives the gyro rotors in the attitude indicator and heading indicator at thousands of RPM. When the pump fails, the suction gauge drops. But the gyros don't stop immediately -- they spin down gradually on residual energy. This means the AI and HI may appear normal for several minutes before precessing to obviously false attitudes. A pilot who doesn't monitor the suction gauge may not realize the AI is drifting until it has diverged significantly from actual aircraft attitude. The turn coordinator is electrically powered -- it survives vacuum failure intact. Partial panel procedure after vacuum failure: navigate using the turn coordinator (bank and rate information), altimeter (altitude), ASI (energy state), and magnetic compass (heading reference with its attendant errors).

**Compass errors: the ones the DPE will test.** The magnetic compass has two systematic error categories in the northern hemisphere. Acceleration errors (ANDS): accelerating on an east or west heading causes the compass to show a false turn toward NORTH. Decelerating on an east or west heading shows a false turn toward SOUTH. Negligible on north/south headings. Turning errors: when rolling through a northerly heading, the compass lags -- the pilot must undershoot (stop the roll early) to actually arrive on north. When rolling through a southerly heading, the compass leads -- the pilot must overshoot to stop on south. The HSI (Horizontal Situation Indicator) is gyro-based and does NOT have these errors -- but it drifts from magnetic north and must be re-synced to the compass every 15 to 20 minutes.

**The checkride trap:** The DPE describes a scenario where the altimeter is frozen, the VSI reads zero, and the airspeed appears to be decreasing in a constant-power climb. 'What has failed and what do you do?' Full analysis: static port is blocked. All three static-connected instruments are affected in exactly this way. Immediate action: select alternate static source if installed. The DPE then asks: 'What effect does alternate static have on the altimeter reading?' Answer: the altimeter over-reads slightly because cabin pressure is lower than outside ambient -- correct for this if shooting any approach using alternate static.
